meta.title: Discover Bahrain
meta.description: The Pearl of the Arabian Gulf: destinations, traditional wear and crafts, nature, cities, 5,000 years of history, celebrations, food and monuments of Bahrain.

welcome.headline: Discover Bahrain
welcome.subheadline: The Pearl of the Arabian Gulf.
welcome.intro: Bahrain is an Arab Muslim kingdom in the middle of the Arabian Gulf, an archipelago of natural islands and artificial islands, with Manama as its capital. Once the capital of the ancient Dilmun civilization, and for thousands of years the home of the world's finest natural pearls, it is a place where 5,000 years of history stand beside gleaming skylines. Its people are known for their generosity and hospitality, and the island is known for its religious tolerance, its poets, its palms and its fresh-water springs.

facts.label: Government
facts.value: Constitutional monarchy; King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa

facts.label: Flag
facts.value: Red and white, separated by a serrated edge of five white points

facts.label: Geography
facts.value: On the western coast of the Arabian Gulf, linked to Saudi Arabia by the King Fahd Causeway (opened 1986). The kingdom includes Bahrain Island (the main island), Muharraq, Sitra, Umm an-Nasan, Hawar and others.

facts.label: Climate
facts.value: Hot and humid summers and mild winters

nicknames.title: Land of Immortality
nicknames.text: From the Sumerian texts about Dilmun in the Epic of Gilgamesh.

welcome.nameOrigin: Bahrain was named after its two types of water: fresh water from natural springs and wells, and the salt water of the surrounding sea.
welcome.wordsIntro: A few words of Bahraini Arabic to start a conversation.

words.say: Shlonak? (to a man) / Shlonich? (to a woman)

didYouKnow: Bahrain was the pearl capital of the world, and pearl diving is a 7,000-year-old profession.
Bahraini ships were built without a single iron nail.
The Bahrain World Trade Center was the first skyscraper in the world to integrate wind turbines.
A tree has survived alone in the Bahraini desert for over 400 years.
Beit Al-Quran holds both the smallest and the largest Quran in the world.
Bahrain was the first Gulf country to discover oil, in 1932.

destinations.title: Interesting Destinations
destinations.intro: An immersive showcase of must-see places. Six destination cards open the page: Qal'at al-Bahrain, the Tree of Life, the Pearling Path, Al-Fateh Grand Mosque, Bahrain World Trade Center and the Old Manama Souq.
destinations.mapLabel: Map of the destinations in Bahrain

featured.title: Qal'at al-Bahrain (Bahrain Fort)
featured.text: Located 4 km west of Manama, it is an archaeological tell: civilizations layered on top of one another for over 4,500 years, from 2300 BCE to the 16th century CE. The fort standing today was built by the Portuguese over the ruins of the Dilmun capital. Visitors see the massive walls, the watchtowers at all four corners and the site museum. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005.
featured.tip: The fort glows at sunset and is lit at night.

featured.title: Tree of Life
featured.text: A Prosopis cineraria tree over 400 years old that stands alone in the desert on a small hill, with no visible water source. Its survival remains a scientific mystery, and it draws tens of thousands of visitors every year. It stands near Jebel Dukhan, the highest point of Bahrain.

featured.title: Pearling Path, Muharraq
featured.text: A 3.5 km walking path through the old city of Muharraq, with 17 historical buildings: homes of pearl merchants (tawawish) and ship captains (nawakhida), Bu Maher Fort and three Hayrats (pearl oyster beds). Famous for authentic Bahraini mud architecture and wooden windows called rawazin. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2012.

featured.title: Al-Fateh Grand Mosque
featured.text: The national mosque of Bahrain, holding 7,000 worshippers. Built in 1988 on an area of 6,500 square metres. It has the largest fibreglass dome in the world (24 m), Kufic calligraphy decorating its walls, Italian marble and a luxurious Austrian chandelier.

featured.title: Bahrain World Trade Center
featured.text: Twin towers 240 metres tall with 50 floors, opened in 2008. The first skyscraper in the world to integrate three massive wind turbines between its towers, generating 11 to 15% of the building's electricity. It won two international awards for sustainable architecture.

featured.title: Old Manama Souq and Bab Al-Bahrain
featured.text: Bab Al-Bahrain, a historic building from 1945, is the symbolic gateway to Manama and its souq. Behind it lies the traditional market famous for spices, incense and oud, perfumes, gold and traditional textiles, including a gold souk.

more.title: Barbar Temple and Dilmun Burial Mounds
more.text: Barbar Temple, in Barbar village, dates to the third millennium BCE and was found in 1954 by a Danish expedition. The Dilmun Burial Mounds hold over 170,000 tombs, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2019.

more.title: Arad Fort
more.text: A 15th-century fort on Muharraq Island beside the sea, with a square shape and circular corner towers, lit at night.

more.title: Hawar Islands
more.text: A group of islands in the south, a protected nature reserve and bird haven.

more.title: Bahrain International Circuit, Sakhir
more.text: Opened in 2004, the first Formula 1 circuit in the Middle East, hosting the annual Bahrain Grand Prix.

wear.title: Traditional Wear

items.title: Thobe (dishdasha)
items.text: A long white robe with long sleeves, worn daily.

items.title: Ghutra
items.text: A white or red checkered head covering.

items.title: Agal
items.text: A doubled black cord worn over the ghutra.

items.title: Bisht
items.text: A luxurious wool cloak worn for occasions, in brown, black or gold.

items.title: Silver dagger
items.text: A dagger decorated with silver and gold, worn on formal occasions.

items.title: Thobe Al-Nashal
items.text: A loose dress of dark silky fabric, embroidered with gold threads on the chest, sleeves and hem.

items.title: Daraa
items.text: A long inner dress with decorated sleeves.

items.title: Bukhnuq
items.text: A young girl's head covering, black embroidered with gold.

items.title: Abaya
items.text: A black outer garment for going out.

items.title: Shaila
items.text: A light black headscarf.

items.title: Burqa
items.text: A traditional face covering, now only worn by elderly women.

items.title: Murtasha
items.text: A long gold necklace set with stones.

items.title: Tassa
items.text: A head ornament.

items.title: Habga
items.text: A necklace with natural pearls.

items.title: Kufuf
items.text: Golden hand ornaments.

items.title: Khulkhal
items.text: An ankle ornament.

items.title: Jalwa
items.text: The first official meeting of the groom and bride.

items.title: Henna
items.text: The bride's hands are decorated with henna among her friends.

items.title: Dazza
items.text: Gifts from the groom's family to the bride.

items.title: Zaffa
items.text: A festive procession with traditional chants.

items.title: Wedding feast
items.text: Quzi, a whole lamb stuffed with chicken, eggs and rice, is the wedding dish.

items.title: Bani Jamra weaving
items.text: A village in northwest Bahrain famous for handwoven cotton and wool on traditional looms, making dishdashas, bishts, women's fabrics and embroidered towels. The weaver sits in an earthen pit with a wooden loom.

items.title: Hand embroidery (Kasheeda)
items.text: A women's craft in traditional homes, embroidering the thobe al-nashal with real gold thread (zari), silver (badla) and buttons (makkook).

items.title: Al-Sadu weaving
items.text: Bedouin weaving of camel and sheep wool into tents, rugs, carpets and saddlebags (kharj), in red, black, white and brown with natural dyes.

items.title: A'ali pottery
items.text: The oldest craft in Bahrain (over 4,000 years), in A'ali village south of Manama near the Dilmun Burial Mounds. Zirs (water jars), burmas (cooking pots), incense burners and vases, made with local red clay, a potter's wheel and stone kilns.

items.title: Shipbuilding
items.text: In Karbabad, Muharraq and Sitra: sailing ships built without iron nails, using only palm-fibre ropes. Types include Boom, Sanbuk, Jalbut, Shuwai, Baghla and Baytil. The main material is teak imported from India.

items.title: Palm-leaf basketry
items.text: In Karbabad, Jannusan and Sar: baskets, mats (hasir), hand fans, hats and brooms made from dried palm fronds and coconut fibre.

items.title: Rope making (Lif)
items.text: In Muharraq and Sitra: strong ropes from coconut and palm fibres, essential for pearl-diving boats.

items.title: Rawazin (wooden windows)
items.text: Carved wooden windows with Arabic and geometric patterns in Muharraq and traditional homes.

items.title: Perfumes, bakhoor and oud
items.text: Oriental perfumes blended with inherited techniques in Manama, Muharraq and all the markets: oud, bakhoor, oud oil, rosewater, amber and musk.

items.title: Decorative ceramics
items.text: Vessels and plates decorated with Islamic patterns.

wear.jewelleryNote: Jewellery is made in 21- and 22-karat gold with natural Bahraini pearls and precious stones, using melting, drawing, soldering, engraving and inlaying. Goldsmiths work in Manama and Muharraq, and the Manama gold souk is the traditional centre.

items.title: Tree of Life
items.text: A Prosopis cineraria tree over 400 years old, alone in the desert with no visible water source. The scientific mystery of its survival is what makes it famous.

items.title: Fresh-water springs
items.text: Bahrain is known for its natural fresh-water springs, including springs that bubble up beneath the sea. They gave the island the name Land of Immortality. The Ain Umm Al-Sujur wells date back to the third millennium BCE.

items.title: Island of a Million Palms
items.text: Palm groves still cover the north-west of the main island, where Bahraini dates, especially the Khalas and Khunaizi varieties, are grown.

items.title: Hawar Islands
items.text: An island group in the south, a protected reserve home to rare birds, including the Socotra cormorant, and to Arabian oryx and gazelles. Day trips and a quiet resort stay.

items.title: Al Areen Wildlife Park and Reserve
items.text: A reserve where Arabian oryx, Bahrain's national animal, and other desert animals can be seen.

items.title: Jebel Dukhan
items.text: The "Mountain of Smoke", about 134 m, the highest point in Bahrain.

items.title: Tubli Bay
items.text: A bay with mangroves and migrating birds close to the capital.

items.title: Beaches and islands
items.text: Al Dar Islands, Amwaj Islands and the shores of the Hawar Islands for swimming and boat trips.

items.title: Desert
items.text: The southern desert around Sakhir, for camping and quad biking under the stars.

items.title: Manama (the capital)
items.text: Bahrain World Trade Center (240 m, 50 floors, three wind turbines); Bahrain Financial Harbour (two towers of 260 m, the tallest buildings in Bahrain, with a modern sail-shaped design); Bab Al-Bahrain and the Old Manama Souq for spices, incense, oud, perfumes, gold and textiles; Al-Fateh Grand Mosque; Bahrain National Museum (opened in 1988 at a cost of $30 million, with 9 galleries covering 6,000 years, Dilmun gold jewellery and archaeological finds); and Beit Al-Quran in Hoora, with rare Quranic manuscripts. Nightlife and dining: Adliya (Block 338) with its cafes, restaurants and art galleries, and the waterfront restaurants of the Financial Harbour.

items.title: Muharraq
items.text: The old capital and heart of the pearling heritage. Walk the Pearling Path, visit Arad Fort, admire the rawazin windows and see shipbuilding and rope making.

items.title: Riffa
items.text: Home of Riffa Fort and the royal family, with desert and modern housing.

items.title: A'ali
items.text: A village south of Manama known for pottery and the Dilmun Burial Mounds.

items.title: Sitra
items.text: An island city known for boat building and an oil port.

items.title: Budaiya
items.text: A coastal town with date farms and old houses on the road along the sea.

items.title: Sakhir
items.text: Home of the Bahrain International Circuit and the Tree of Life area.

history.title: History
history.intro: A history of 5,000 years. Bahrain was home to three great civilizations: Dilmun, Tylos and Awal.

timeline.text: Dilmun: a global trading centre linking Mesopotamia (Iraq) with the Indus Valley (India), famous for copper, dates and pearls. The Sumerians called it the Land of Immortality in the Epic of Gilgamesh.
Bahrain becomes known as Tylos in the Greek and Roman period, an important trading post on the route of Alexander the Great.
Bahrain is known as Awal, a name derived from an idol worshipped on the island.
Bahrain embraces Islam peacefully, during the time of the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH).
Al-Khamis Mosque, the oldest mosque in Bahrain, is built.
The Portuguese take Bahrain and build the fort at Qal'at al-Bahrain.
Sheikh Ahmed bin Muhammad Al-Fateh Al Khalifa founds the modern state; the Al Khalifa family still rules.
Treaties with Britain place Bahrain under British protection.
Al-Hidaya Al-Khalifiya School opens in Muharraq, the first regular school in Bahrain.
The Muharraq Literary Club is founded.
The first girls' school in the Gulf opens in Muharraq.
The pearl trade declines after the arrival of cultured pearls.
Oil is discovered, a first for the Gulf, starting a new era for the economy.
The Bahrain International Circuit opens: the first Formula 1 circuit in the Middle East.
Qal'at al-Bahrain, the Pearling Path and the Dilmun Burial Mounds are inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

pearl.title: Pearl and maritime heritage
pearl.intro: Before oil, pearls were the lifeblood of Bahrain. Pearl diving is a 7,000-year-old profession and Bahrain was once the pearl capital of the world.

groups.title: Diving seasons
groups.text: Khanjiya (pre-season); Al-Ghaws Al-Kabeer, the Great Dive, 4 months from May to September; Al-Radda, a short return season; Al-Rdedia, the final season.

groups.title: Roles on the ship
groups.text: Nokhada: the captain. Ghais: the diver. Saib: pulls the diver up with the rope. Tawwash: the pearl merchant. Nahham: the singer of sea chants.

groups.title: Diving tools
groups.text: Fatam: a wooden clip for the nose. Diyeen: a fibre basket for oysters. Zabil: a rope weighted with a stone. Khabt: a knife to open oysters. Mashkhal: used to sort pearls.

groups.title: Types of pearls
groups.text: Danah: the highest quality and most valuable. Hasbaa: medium. Badla: smaller. Yakka: the smallest.

groups.title: Sea arts
groups.text: Fijiri: the sailors' chanted art with drums and tambourine. Sawt: traditional music with the oud. Tanboura: an ancient lyre. Liwa: a communal dance with African-infused rhythms.

figures.name: Sheikh Ahmed bin Muhammad Al-Fateh Al Khalifa
figures.text: Founder of the modern state of Bahrain in 1783.

figures.name: Sheikh Isa bin Ali Al Khalifa
figures.text: A long-reigning ruler whose Muharraq house is a heritage site.

figures.name: Sheikh Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa
figures.text: The ruler who led Bahrain to independence in 1971.

figures.name: King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa
figures.text: The current king; Bahrain became a kingdom in 2002.

figures.name: Sheikh Ibrahim bin Muhammad Al Khalifa
figures.text: Known as "the Sheikh of Writers", a pioneer of the literary renaissance who founded the Muharraq Literary Club in 1920 and helped establish Al-Hidaya Al-Khalifiya School.

figures.name: Ibrahim Al-Arrayedh
figures.text: "The Prince of Poets" in Bahrain, who wrote many diwans and poetic plays and taught a generation of Bahraini poets.

figures.name: Sheikh Ahmed bin Muhammad Al Khalifa
figures.text: The poet of nature in Bahrain, a student of Al-Arrayedh.

figures.name: Qassim Haddad
figures.text: A contemporary poet whose works have been translated into French, English and German.

figures.name: Sheikh Yusuf bin Ahmed Al-Siddiqi
figures.text: Judge and preacher at Al-Qudhaibiya Mosque, an Al-Azhar graduate and one of the great scholars of 20th-century Bahrain.

figures.name: Sheikha Mai bint Mohammed Al Khalifa
figures.text: A scholar and writer who chaired the Bahrain Authority for Culture and Antiquities and led the inscription of Bahrain's sites on the UNESCO lists.

figures.name: Abdullah Al-Muharraqi
figures.text: A pioneer of fine art whose paintings portray heritage and the marine environment.

figures.name: Nasser Al-Yousif
figures.text: A late Bahraini artist whose oil paintings document old everyday life.

figures.name: Mohammed Zuwaid and Ali Bahar
figures.text: Pioneers of Bahraini music, in particular the sawt art; Sultan Hameed and Khalid Al-Sheikh are also leading names.

figures.name: Winfred Yavi, Ruth Jebet and Maryam Yusuf Jamal
figures.text: Olympic gold medallists in athletics for Bahrain (Yavi in the 3000 m steeplechase in Paris 2024, with an Olympic record).

items.title: Labour Day
items.text: Celebrates workers.

items.title: National Day
items.text: The national celebration of the kingdom, with official ceremonies, parades, fireworks and lit-up cities. It is linked to Bahrain's independence in 1971.

items.title: Accession Day
items.text: Follows National Day; the two days form a national holiday.

items.title: Eid al-Fitr
items.text: Three days at the end of Ramadan. Khabeesa and Bahraini halwa are prepared, families visit one another and children receive Eidiya (Eid money).

items.title: Arafat Day and Eid al-Adha
items.text: The feast of sacrifice.

items.title: Islamic New Year (Al Hijra)
items.text: The first day of the Hijri calendar.

items.title: Ashura
items.text: The 9th and 10th of Muharram, observed with religious gatherings and processions.

items.title: The Prophet's Birthday
items.text: Celebrated with religious gatherings.

items.title: Gargee'an
items.text: Celebrated on the 14th and 15th nights of Ramadan. Children wear colourful traditional Bahraini clothing and go from house to house singing traditional chants. Neighbours welcome them with candies, nuts and dried fruits in decorated bags.

items.title: Chant of Gargee'an
items.text: "Gargee'an Gargee'an, give us and may God give to you, may He take you to the House of Mecca, O Mecca, O the flourishing, O mother of chains and gold, O Nora."

items.title: Naqsa
items.text: Neighbours exchange dishes during Ramadan.

items.title: Reyouq
items.text: The iftar breakfast, with balaleet and nakhi.

items.title: Suhoor
items.text: Preceded by the Musaharati, who walks the streets with his drum.

items.title: Cannons
items.text: The iftar and imsak cannons are daily rituals.

items.title: The Majlis (Diwaniya)
items.text: A sitting room in the home for receiving guests, where coffee and dates are served and conversation is shared.

items.title: Bahrain Grand Prix
items.text: The annual Formula 1 race at the Bahrain International Circuit in Sakhir.

items.title: Camel racing
items.text: A traditional sport of the desert.

items.title: Sea heritage
items.text: Fijiri, sawt and liwa performances keep the pearl-diving songs and dances alive.

weddings.title: Weddings
weddings.text: Bahraini weddings include the jalwa (the first official meeting of the groom and bride), the henna night, the dazza (gifts from the groom's family) and the zaffa (a festive procession with traditional chants), followed by a feast of quzi.

food.eyebrow: The sea and the palm grove
food.title: Best Foods
food.intro: Bahraini cuisine relies on the bounty of the sea and the palm groves and reflects the values of generosity and hospitality.

items.title: Machboos (the national dish)
items.text: Basmati rice cooked in a spiced broth (cloves, cardamom, turmeric, cinnamon) with meat, chicken or fish. Served at celebrations and feasts.

items.title: Muhammar (sweet rice)
items.text: One of the most distinctive rice dishes in Bahrain. Rice sweetened with dates, sugar, cardamom and saffron, dark brown in colour. Always served with fried fish (safi or hamour). Sweet meets savoury.

items.title: Harees
items.text: Cracked wheat cooked with meat for hours until smooth like porridge. Served hot with ghee or melted butter and a sprinkle of sugar and cinnamon. A Ramadan staple.

items.title: Balaleet
items.text: Sweet vermicelli with saffron, cardamom and sugar, topped with an egg omelette. A traditional breakfast (reyouq) that combines sweet and savoury.

items.title: Luqaimat
items.text: Small dough balls fried until golden, dipped in date syrup (dibs) with cardamom and saffron. One of the most popular Ramadan sweets.

items.title: Quzi
items.text: A whole lamb stuffed with chicken, eggs and rice, grilled over charcoal. A wedding dish.

items.title: Mahyawa
items.text: A strong fermented fish sauce, served with flatbread.

items.title: Mumawash
items.text: Rice with green lentils and dried shrimp.

items.title: Nakhi
items.text: Soaked and boiled chickpeas with chilli pepper and cumin.

items.title: Bajela
items.text: Boiled green fava beans with salt.

items.title: Khabeesa
items.text: A sweet of flour, ghee, sugar and cardamom.

items.title: Halwa Showaiter
items.text: A brown, translucent sweet made of starch and sugar, the most famous popular dessert.

coffee.title: Arabic coffee
coffee.text: The dallah (golden coffee pot) and the small finjan cups are symbols of Bahraini hospitality. The coffee is roasted with cardamom and saffron and served with dates.
coffee.etiquette: Etiquette: shake the cup slightly when you have had enough.

food.products: Bahraini dates (Khalas and Khunaizi), natural pearls (Danah), traditional sweets such as Bahraini halwa and khabeesa, and oriental perfumes, bakhoor and oud.

monuments.title: Monuments & Historical Spots
monuments.intro: Bahrain has three UNESCO World Heritage sites.

items.title: Qal'at al-Bahrain
items.text: The ancient capital of Dilmun and a Portuguese fort, with layers of 4,500 years of history, massive walls and a site museum.

items.title: Pearling Path, Muharraq
items.text: A 3.5 km path of 17 buildings, including merchants' houses, Bu Maher Fort and the pearl oyster beds; the Siyadi House and Shaikh Isa bin Ali House are part of the heritage of Muharraq.

items.title: Dilmun Burial Mounds
items.text: Over 170,000 tombs, among the largest ancient burial grounds in the world.

items.title: Barbar Temple
items.text: Third millennium BCE temple found in 1954 by a Danish expedition. Dedicated to Enki, the Sumerian god of water, with a stone altar, a sacred well and stairs leading to the spring.

items.title: Saar settlement
items.text: An ancient residential city of the Dilmun period.

items.title: Ain Umm Al-Sujur
items.text: Wells dating to the third millennium BCE.

items.title: Arad Fort
items.text: A 15th-century fort on Muharraq Island, square in shape with circular corner towers.

items.title: Riffa Fort
items.text: A fort built in 1812 on a ridge in Riffa.

items.title: Bu Maher Fort
items.text: A fort on the Pearling Path, on the sea.

items.title: Al-Khamis Mosque
items.text: The oldest mosque in Bahrain, from the 7th century, in the reign of the Umayyad Caliph Umar ibn Abdul Aziz, with twin matching minarets that are a unique feature in Islamic architecture.

items.title: Bab Al-Bahrain
items.text: A historic building from 1945, the gateway to Old Manama.

items.title: Bahrain National Museum
items.text: Opened in 1988 with 9 galleries covering 6,000 years of history.

items.title: Beit Al-Quran
items.text: A museum and library in Hoora with a rare collection of Quranic manuscripts, the smallest Quran in the world and the largest Quran in the world.

items.title: Al-Fateh Grand Mosque
items.text: The national mosque, built in 1988, with the largest fibreglass dome in the world.
